title: 7 Reasons Why You Shouldn't Lecture Your Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Opening with a vignette of a teacher pulling a student off the playground for a scolding, Linsin makes the case that lecturing misbehaving students is a counterproductive habit even though it can feel effective in the moment. He lists seven reasons lecturing backfires: it's stressful for the teacher, it substitutes for real accountability, it can sabotage the accountability of an already-assigned consequence, it invites students to argue, it breeds resentment, it eats up instructional time, and ultimately words carry less weight than consistent action. He recommends replacing lectures with a terse statement of the rule broken followed by enforcement of a consequence. The article closes by asserting that letting accountability—not talk—do the teaching produces lessons students actually internalize.
points: Lecturing feels effective short-term but is one of the biggest sources of teacher stress and burnout.
A lecture on the way to time-out can feel like a 'double consequence' to students, breeding resentment instead of reflection.
Lecturing invites argument—backing a student into a corner tempts even compliant students to fight back.
Say only what rule was broken, enforce the consequence, and move on; let accountability do the teaching.
Actions consistently carry more behavioral weight with students than words ever will.
quotes: So you run out, pull Anthony off the playground, and let him have it. You give him a fire-breathing, finger-pointing, he’s-got-it-comin’ lecture, topped off with a stern, “Do you understand me?

Using words to try and convince students to behave is perhaps the number one cause of stress among teachers. And because lecturing kinda-sorta works in the short term, teachers feel encouraged to keep on doing it—despite the tension headaches.
When you lecture, you all but dare your students to argue with you . In fact, it takes a strong-willed student not to.
Your words will never carry as much weight as your actions. And the longer students are in school, the more this is true.
Simply tell the student what rule was broken, then enforce a consequence and move on to more important things—like teaching your class.
